description: The museum's own page and the FAA registration both give 44-84410 with an RAAF history as A68-706 but MustangsMustangs traces N83KD to P-51D-25-NA 44-73260 which was surplus at McClellan AFB in 1958 then a Cavalier demonstrator remanufactured 1969 and exported to the Indonesian Air Force as F-361 before being recovered from wreckage in Java in 1979; the construction number 122-39719 maps arithmetically to 44-73260 and cannot belong to 44-84410 which is the decisive check; painted as 353rd Fighter Group 350th Fighter Squadron LH-O

Composite airframe rebuilt at Kissimmee Florida in 1988 using the centre section of 44-28765; built at Kansas City and ready August 1945 but placed straight into storage at Altus as the B-25 contract had been cancelled; removed 1948 and converted to TB-25N pilot trainer serving at Bolling Kelly Offutt and Wright-Patterson; disposed of 1959 and flew as Axis Nightmare before the museum bought it in 2004

Lend-leased to the RNZAF as NZ3119; damaged in a landing-gear collapse in training with 16 Squadron at Woodbourne then used as a squadron hack; sold for scrap March 1948 and rescued from a New Zealand scrapyard; structurally rebuilt in Auckland and delivered to Cincinnati February 2008 with first flight 2011; returned to flight July 2016 after an accident and was 2016 EAA AirVenture WWII Grand Champion; the museum's own page prints NZ3119 in the serial field which is the RNZAF serial not the USAAF one
aliases: Kittyhawk; Warhawk; NZ3119; N5813; c/n 27501; P40; P40M

description: Accepted by the Navy 26 May 1945 and saw no combat; struck 1955 with 1533 hours; saved by Ed Maloney in 1958 and used as a roadside advertisement for the fledgling Planes of Fame; bought by David Tallichet 1973 and made airworthy 1975 and used in the Baa Baa Black Sheep television series; the museum states it has been in storage since 1977
aliases: F4U; Corsair; BuNo 92132; N3466G; FG1; FG1D

description: Reproduction and not an original airframe; built by Flug Werk GmbH of Munich as one of a run of 21 based on the data plate of an Arado-built Fw 190 F-8/R1 written off in combat in 1944 with a few parts recovered from the crash site in 2000 incorporated; re-engined with a Pratt and Whitney R-2800-57M2; donated by Dr Thomas Summer in December 2007 and completed 2019 with first flight November 2019; the FAA year of 1944 reflects the donor data plate not the date this airframe was built

Arrived at the museum by air on 8 March 2025 and is confirmed present by the museum's own arrival video; the museum's own specification block prints Serial Number 51-017 which is not a US military serial for this aircraft while its narrative text gives Bureau Number 149836 matching the FAA record; the FAA YEAR-MFR of 1951 is irreconcilable with that BuNo so year_built is left blank
aliases: UF-1; SA-16; Albatross; BuNo 149836; N7026C; HU16; HU16C; UF1; SA16

description: Built at Dallas and delivered to the USAAF 15 May 1944; served in New York Alabama Georgia Louisiana Minnesota Nebraska Texas and North Carolina; to storage October 1953 and surplus two years later; sold in 1958 with 5098 hours and restored over ten years by Ron Klemm of Fairbanks Alaska before sale to the museum in 1999
aliases: T-6; SNJ; Harvard; Texan; N7RK; AT6; AT6D; T6

description: Delivered to the USAAF 5 February 1945 as a C-45F then returned to Beech in 1951 and almost entirely rebuilt with only the outer wings tail and a few fuselage parts reused; back to the USAF 1952 and stored 1959; sold to Busby's Bowling Lanes of Odessa Texas in 1960 and later owned by Virginia Tech before being bought for the museum in 2014; the FAA calls it a TC-45G while the museum calls it a TC-45H and AF-86 is the Beech remanufacture number not a USAF serial
aliases: TC-45G; C-45F; Beech 18; AF-86; N7826L; TC45; TC45H; TC45G; C45F; AF86

description: Delivered to the US Navy 9 June 1943 for primary training at NAS Memphis and NAS Bunker Hill then to NAS Ottumwa and stricken 31 October 1946; crashed August 1958 and stored for years before restoration by Pete Jones of Air Repair in May 1991 for David Funk with new wooden wings; bought by the museum in 2005; the museum titles the page PT-17 but its own text and the Navy BuNo make it an N2S
aliases: PT-17; Kaydet; Stearman; Model 75; B75N1; BuNo 38278; c/n 75-7899; N224DF; PT17

description: Completed as an L-4H on 20 July 1943 and delivered two days later then flown to Camp Rucker in August; struck 15 February 1945 and passed to the Reconstruction Finance Corporation; restored by Patrick McGuiness and donated to the museum in 2020 by his grandson David Zitt; the FAA serial 10623 is the Piper construction number not the military serial
aliases: J-3; Grasshopper; Cub; c/n 10623; N20PM; L4; L4H; J3

description: Completed as a J3C-65 on 13 January 1947 and therefore not one of the 51 genuine 1941 Flitfires; it is finished in Flitfire silver and RAF roundel presentation; bought by volunteer Dennis Stewart in 2017 and given to the museum in honour of his father becoming the museum's tenth flyable aircraft in December 2021; the FAA currently returns N3513N as not assigned which suggests the registration has lapsed since

Listed on the museum's own aircraft index and flown in the museum's 2025 Warbird Flying Showcase but privately owned; the FAA shows N51122 registered to Michael S. Durkee of Amelia Ohio as a Ryan Aeronautical ST3KR serial 2204 with YEAR-MFR 1942; included because the museum presents it as part of its collection
